{"self_assessment": "Impact: I owned the fish's tail, the loop that gives the picture its fish identity, and laid it from the crossing in the middle out to the far end, closing the loop back toward the belly. With the body outline, that tail is what makes the judge read a fish rather than a leaf, and about 108 of 111 dominoes were connected to the start for the push.

Execution: I laid the tail stroke steadily from the middle crossing, picking it up once the body lines arrived, and finished it with time to spare. I inspected the area twice and stood a fallen domino back up so the tail stayed connected. Then I kept my hands off the finished work so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed with regular updates on the tail and the overall state of the fish. I stayed clear of the nose and the middle crossing so I wouldn't collide with teammates working there, and I flagged the small sideways offset I noticed at the crossing so the person responsible for it could handle it. I backed Sofia's fish idea early and kept morale high through the final minutes.

Leadership: I committed quickly to the fish plan and took a stroke without being asked twice, which helped the table move fast. I kept energy up as the clock ran down and encouraged everyone to stay hands-off for a clean push. I believe the tail was a central piece of the result, though the body lines and the nose joint were also essential, and the fish worked because all of it connected.", "my_share_percent": 30}
